findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the endpoint's datetime sort key and will 500
findings.body: The endpoint orders by "-datetime" but OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits Paginator's key handling: get_item_key (src/sentry/api/paginator.py:838-840) computes int(math.floor(value)) on a datetime, which raises TypeError, and value_from_cursor (line 842) returns the raw millisecond integer from the cursor and passes it into a WHERE clause comparing a timestamp column to a bigint ("datetime <= 1234567890123"), which Postgres rejects with an operator-does-not-exist error. Unlike DateTimePaginator, this class never converts between datetimes and the ms-epoch cursor representation. Consequently, any request with optimized_pagination=true from a superuser or globally-access member against a non-empty audit log will raise an unhandled exception and return a 500 instead of a page of results.

findings.title: Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises AssertionError; the 'advanced feature' can never work
findings.body: The negative-offset path in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result (lines 877-882) slices the queryset as queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start_offset. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — the ORM raises "AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported" — so this branch always errors instead of returning results. The code comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Since the cursor string ("value:offset:is_prev") is client-controlled and Cursor.from_string happily parses negative offsets, any client hitting this endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and a crafted cursor such as "0:-5:0" triggers an unhandled exception / 500. There is no valid input for which this feature works.

findings.title: BasePaginator change claims to support negative offsets but still crashes for is_prev cursors, and silently changes behavior otherwise
findings.body: The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps negative offsets for forward cursors; for previous-page cursors a negative client-supplied offset still flows into queryset[start_offset:stop] and raises Django's "Negative indexing is not supported" AssertionError, contradicting the comment that negative offsets are now allowed. For forward cursors, the clamp silently changes existing behavior: a malformed cursor like "0:-50:0" that previously errored now returns the first page, and the unclamped negative offset is still passed into build_cursor via the original cursor object, so the generated next/prev cursors can carry bogus negative offsets forward. Either validate the offset (reject negatives) or handle both directions consistently.

findings.title: Client-toggled paginator class breaks cursor portability between requests
findings.body: The paginator implementation now depends on a per-request query parameter (optimized_pagination) plus who is calling, so the same endpoint issues cursors with different semantics depending on the request. A cursor produced by DateTimePaginator encodes a ms-epoch value that DateTimePaginator converts back to a datetime for its WHERE clause; if the same cursor is replayed against OptimizedCursorPaginator (same user toggles the flag, or a superuser shares a link with a non-superuser), the raw integer is compared against the timestamp column and the request errors or returns wrong rows. Pagination cursors are supposed to be opaque tokens valid for the endpoint; making their interpretation depend on a mutable flag violates that contract and will produce intermittent 500s/incorrect pages for clients.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator's non-negative path is a verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result and provides no performance benefit
findings.body: Apart from the broken negative-offset branch, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates BasePaginator.get_result line for line (same build_queryset, same slicing, same cursor building). The PR is titled 'Enhanced Pagination Performance for High-Volume Audit Logs', but for every working request the query plan and workload are identical to the existing DateTimePaginator path — no index hints, no query reduction, nothing. The class adds ~100 lines of duplicated pagination logic (which will drift from the base implementation, as it already has with the misleading comments) with no measurable gain, while the only genuinely new behavior (negative offsets) is a guaranteed exception. The feature should either be justified with a real optimization or removed.

findings.title: Admin-gated 'advanced features' flag is security theater with a misleading safety comment
findings.body: The gating `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` combined with the comment "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" implies the advanced path exposes something extra that permissions must guard. It does not: pagination offsets never bypass queryset filters, and the only 'advanced' capability (negative offsets) is an error path in the ORM. Meanwhile, the flag does create a real inconsistency: a superuser and a regular owner hitting the same URL with the same cursor get different paginator semantics (and, per the other findings, a 500 vs. working results). If there is no concrete capability being gated, remove the flag and the misleading comments rather than implying there is a privileged pagination mode.

findings.title: No tests for the new paginator, the negative-offset path, or the endpoint's optimized branch
findings.body: The PR adds a new paginator class, modifies the shared BasePaginator.get_result used by many endpoints, and adds a new request-parameter-driven branch on a production endpoint, but includes no tests. At minimum it needs: (1) a regression test that BasePaginator.get_result behavior is unchanged for existing cursors (including the new max(0, offset) clamp), (2) tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator covering forward/prev cursors, which would have immediately caught the datetime TypeError and the Django negative-slicing AssertionError, and (3) endpoint tests covering the optimized_pagination flag for both authorized and unauthorized users.

findings.title: Comment-only change documents behavior that does not exist
findings.body: The only change in cursors.py is a comment asserting "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" above `self.offset = int(offset)`. The line of code is unchanged — Cursor has always accepted any int, and nothing in this file enables or handles negative offsets. Worse, downstream consumers (build_cursor's _build_next_values/_build_prev_values) compute new offsets via `offset + limit` / `offset - limit` with no lower bound, so negative offsets propagate into emitted cursors. The comment misleads readers into thinking negative-offset support was added and validated here; it should be removed or replaced with a note that offsets are unvalidated.
